summary: Adds a way in the Session Description Protocol to describe attributes of individual media sources inside a single media stream, such as separate RTP sources that share one session. Plain SDP could only describe whole streams, so this fills in the gap.

plainLanguage.summary:
An SDP description tells a receiver about a media session: which addresses to use and which codecs to expect. It describes the session as a whole and each media stream in it, but it stops there.

This document adds a third level, below the media stream, so that each individual source of media inside a stream can be named and described. That matters when one participant sends from more than one camera, and when a receiver needs to know which streams are copies of each other.

questions: describe individual rtp sources in sdp
what is the sdp ssrc attribute
how to describe multiple rtp sources in sdp
subtitle: Adds SDP attributes that describe the individual media sources inside one media stream, not just the stream as a whole.

tldr.problem: SDP describes a multimedia session and the media streams inside it, but it has no way to describe the individual sources inside one media stream. RTP allows several sources in a session, for example a user with more than one camera, and single-source multicast needs to name them so that identifiers do not collide.
tldr.mechanism: Two new media-level attributes are defined. The ssrc attribute names a source by its 32-bit synchronization source identifier and attaches a source-level attribute to it, such as cname. The ssrc-group attribute lists several source identifiers that stand in a defined relationship, such as FID for retransmission.
tldr.outcome: Receivers learn which sources exist, how they relate and which canonical name each one uses, and the rules for SSRC collisions and for reusing identifiers are tightened. Because SDP readers ignore unknown attributes, endpoints must assume a receiver may not understand the new lines.

facts.label: ssrc attribute form
facts.value: a=ssrc: then the id, then the attribute

today: RFC 5576 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the ssrc and ssrc-group SDP media-level attributes, and creates two IANA registries within the SDP parameters registry: one for source-level attributes and one for source grouping semantics.

sections.title: Why Sources Need Their Own Description
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol of RFC 4566 provides mechanisms to describe attributes of multimedia sessions and of individual media streams, for example Real-time Transport Protocol sessions within a multimedia session, but it provides no mechanism to describe individual media sources within a media stream.

Several recently proposed protocols, notably RTP single-source multicast, have found it useful to describe specific media sources in SDP messages. Single-source multicast in particular needs to ensure that the receiver's RTP synchronization source identifiers do not collide with those of the media senders, as the RTP specification requires that colliding sources change their identifier after a collision has been detected. Earlier work has used mechanisms specific to each protocol to describe the individual sources of an RTP session.

Moreover, whereas RTP is defined as allowing multiple sources in an RTP session, for example if a user has more than one camera, SDP has no existing mechanism for an endpoint to indicate that it will be using multiple sources or to describe their characteristics individually.

This document defines a mechanism to describe RTP sources, identified by their synchronization source identifier, in SDP, to associate attributes with these sources, and to express relationships among individual sources. It also defines a number of new SDP attributes that apply to individual sources, which the RFC calls source-level attributes, describes how a number of existing media-level attributes can also be applied at the source level, and establishes IANA registries for source-level attributes and for source grouping semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: RTP lets one session carry several separate sources, such as two cameras from the same person. SDP could not say so. This document fills that gap and adds a way to say that two sources are related, for example that one is a retransmission of the other.

sections.title: Session Level, Media Level and Source Level
sections.content:
In RTP, an association among a group of communicating participants is known as an RTP session. An RTP session is typically associated with a single transport address, in the case of multicast, or communication flow, in the case of unicast, though RTP translators and single-source multicast can make the situation more complex.

Within an RTP session, the source of a single stream of RTP packets is known as a synchronization source, and every synchronization source is identified by a 32-bit numeric identifier. Receivers, who may never send RTP packets, also have source identifiers, used to identify their RTCP receiver reports and other feedback messages.

An SDP session description describes a multimedia session, which is a set of multimedia senders and receivers along with the data streams flowing from senders to receivers. A multimedia session contains a number of media streams, the individual RTP sessions or other media paths over which one type of multimedia data is carried. Information that applies to an entire multimedia session is session-level information, while information pertaining to one media stream is media-level information. The collection of all the information describing a media stream is a media description, sometimes known informally as an SDP m-line. Several standard information elements are defined at both the session level and the media level, and extended information can be included at both levels through the use of attributes.

The core SDP specification has no way of describing individual media sources, particularly RTP synchronization sources, within a media stream. This document introduces a third level of information, called source-level information. Syntactically, source-level information is described by a new SDP media-level attribute, ssrc, which identifies specific synchronization sources within an RTP session and acts as a meta-attribute mapping source-level attribute information to these sources. A second new media-level attribute, ssrc-group, represents relationships among media sources within an RTP session in much the same way as the group attribute represents relationships among media streams within a multimedia session.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three levels of description. The session level covers everything in the call, the media level covers one stream of media, and this document adds a source level below that for each individual sender inside a stream.

sections.title: The ssrc and ssrc-group Media Attributes
sections.content:
The ssrc media attribute has the form a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> <attribute> or a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> <attribute>:<value>. It indicates a property of a media source within an RTP session. The ssrc-id is the synchronization source identifier of the source being described, interpreted as a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order and represented in decimal. The attribute or attribute:value is the source-level attribute specific to that source, and it follows the syntax of the SDP a= line, so it consists of either a single attribute name acting as a flag, or an attribute name and value such as cname:user@example.com. No attributes of the flag-only type are defined by this document.

Within a media stream, ssrc attributes with the same ssrc-id describe different attributes of the same media source. Across media streams, ssrc-id values are not correlated, unless correlation is indicated by media-stream grouping or some other mechanism, and MAY be repeated. For each source mentioned in SDP, the source-level attribute cname MUST be provided, and any number of other source-level attributes MAY also be provided. The attribute MAY be used for any RTP-based media transport and is not defined for other transports. If other SDP attributes also mention RTP SSRC values, for example in the MIKEY attribute, the values used MUST be consistent.

The formal grammar is ssrc-attr = "ssrc:" ssrc-id SP attribute, where ssrc-id = integer covers 0 to 2**32 - 1. The ssrc media attribute is not dependent on charset.

The ssrc-group media attribute has the form a=ssrc-group:<semantics> <ssrc-id> .... It expresses a relationship among several sources of an RTP session, and is analogous to the group session-level attribute, which expresses a relationship among media streams in a multimedia session. As sources are already identified by their SSRC identifiers, no analogous property to the mid attribute is necessary; groups of sources are identified by their SSRC identifiers directly.

The semantics parameter is taken from the specification of the group attribute. The initial semantic values defined for ssrc-group are FID, Flow Identification, and FEC, Forward Error Correction. In each case, the relationship among the grouped sources is the same as the relationship among corresponding sources in media streams grouped using the SDP group attribute. The other group semantics registered with IANA are not useful for source grouping: LS, Lip Synchronization, is redundant for sources within a media stream, as RTP sources with the same CNAME are implicitly synchronized in RTP; SRF, Single Reservation Flow, and ANAT, Alternative Network Address Types, refer specifically to the media stream's transport characteristics; and CS, Composite Session, is used to group FLUTE sessions, so it is not applicable to RTP.

The attribute indicates the sources in a group by listing their ssrc-ids. It MUST list at least one ssrc-id for a group and MAY list any number of additional ones, and every ssrc-id listed MUST be defined by a corresponding ssrc line in the same media description. The formal grammar is ssrc-group-attr = "ssrc-group:" semantics *(SP ssrc-id) with semantics = "FEC" / "FID" / token. The ssrc-group media attribute is not dependent on charset.
sections.plainLanguage: The ssrc line names one source and says something about it. The ssrc-group line lists several sources and names the way they relate, for example that one is a retransmission copy of another. Every source listed in a group must also have its own ssrc line in the same part of the description.

sections.title: Using the Identified Sources in RTP
sections.content:
The synchronization source identifiers used in an RTP session are chosen randomly and independently by endpoints, so it is possible for two endpoints to choose the same identifier. The probability is low, but the RTP specification requires that all endpoints MUST be prepared to detect and resolve collisions. All endpoints MUST therefore be prepared for the fact that information about specific sources identified in a media stream might be out of date; the actual binding between SSRCs and source CNAMEs can only be identified by the source description RTCP packets transmitted on the RTP session.

When endpoints choose their own local SSRC values for media streams for which source-level attributes have been specified, they MUST NOT use for themselves any SSRC identifiers mentioned in media descriptions they have received for that media stream. Sources identified by SDP source-level attributes do not otherwise affect RTP transport logic: sources that are only known through SDP, for which neither RTP nor RTCP packets have been received, MUST NOT be counted for RTP group size estimation, and report blocks MUST NOT be sent for them in SR or RR RTCP messages. Endpoints MUST NOT assume that only the sources mentioned in SDP will be present in an RTP session, because additional sources with previously unmentioned SSRC identifiers can be added at any time.

An endpoint that observes an SSRC collision between its explicitly signaled source and another entity that has not explicitly signaled an SSRC MAY delay its RTP collision-resolution actions by 5*1.5*Td, where Td is the deterministic calculated reporting interval for receivers, to see whether the conflict still exists. This gives precedence to explicitly signaled sources and places the burden of collision resolution on non-signaled sources. Collisions between multiple explicitly signaled sources, however, MUST be acted upon immediately.

If a source identified by source-level attributes has been forced to change its SSRC identifier, the author of the SDP SHOULD send out an updated session description with the new SSRC if the mechanism distributing the SDP can distribute updates. That updated description MUST include a previous-ssrc source-level attribute listing the source's previous identifier. If only a single source with a given CNAME has collided, the other session members can infer a correspondence between the old and new identifiers without an updated description, but if more than one source collides at once, or if sources are leaving and rejoining, that inference is not possible. Sending updated descriptions is therefore always RECOMMENDED.

Endpoints MUST NOT reuse the same SSRC identifier for identified sources with the same CNAME for at least the duration of the RTP session's participant timeout interval, and SHOULD NOT reuse any SSRC identifier ever mentioned in SDP for the entire lifetime of the RTP session.
sections.plainLanguage:
Because the numbers that name sources are picked at random, two devices can pick the same one. The rules here make sure a device does not steal a number that somebody else has already advertised, and that it notices when the description it holds has gone out of date.

When a source really does have to change its number, the description is sent again with the new number and a note of the old one.

sections.title: The Source-Level Attributes
sections.content:
The cname source attribute, written a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> cname:<cname>, associates a media source with its Canonical End-Point Identifier source description item. This MUST be the CNAME value that the media sender will place in its RTCP source description packets, and it therefore MUST follow the syntax conventions of CNAME defined in the RTP specification. If a session participant receives an RTCP source description packet associating this SSRC with a different CNAME, it SHOULD assume there has been an SSRC collision and that the description of the source carried in the SDP is not applicable to the actual source being received. This attribute is REQUIRED to be present if any source attributes are present for a source, and MUST NOT occur more than once for the same ssrc-id within a given media stream. Its grammar is cname-attr = "cname:" cname, and it is not dependent on charset.

The previous-ssrc source attribute, written a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> previous-ssrc:<ssrc-id> ..., associates a media source with previous source identifiers used for the same media source. Following an SSRC change due to a collision involving a source described in SDP, the updated session description MUST include it, associating the new SSRC with the old one. If further updated descriptions are published, it SHOULD be included if the description was generated before the participant timeout of the old SSRC, and MAY be included after that point. If present, it MUST list at least one previous SSRC and MAY list any number of additional ones if the source has collided more than once, and it MUST be present only once for each source. Its grammar is previous-ssrc-attr = "previous-ssrc:" ssrc-id *(SP ssrc-id), and it is not dependent on charset.

The fmtp source attribute, written a=ssrc:<ssrc> fmtp:<format> <format specific parameters>, allows format-specific parameters to be conveyed about a given source. The format parameter MUST be one of the media formats, that is, the RTP payload types, specified for the media stream, and the meaning of the format-specific parameters is unique for each media type. This parameter MUST only be used for media types for which source-level format parameters have explicitly been specified; media-level format parameters MUST NOT be carried over blindly. It is not dependent on charset.

The document defines only source attributes that are necessary or useful for an endpoint to decode and render the sources in a media stream. It does not include attributes that would contribute to a decision to accept or reject a stream, for example in an offer/answer exchange; those are left for future consideration. All source-level attributes MUST be registered with IANA in the new registry for source-level attributes, and the initial contents of that registry are cname, previous-ssrc and fmtp.
sections.plainLanguage: Three attributes are defined for a source. The cname gives the canonical name the sender will use for itself, which must be present whenever any source attribute is present. The previous-ssrc records identifiers the source has used before, after a collision. The fmtp carries codec parameters that apply to one source only.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The first example shows an audio stream advertising a single source:

m=audio 49168 RTP/AVP 0
a=ssrc:314159 cname:user@example.com

The second example shows a video stream where one participant, identified by a single CNAME, has several cameras:

m=video 49170 RTP/AVP 96
a=rtpmap:96 H264/90000
a=ssrc:12345 cname:another-user@example.com
a=ssrc:67890 cname:another-user@example.com

The sources could be further distinguished by RTCP source description information.

The third example shows how the relationships among sources used for RTP retransmission can be explicitly signalled, with two groups of two sources, each marked FID:

m=video 49174 RTP/AVPF 96 98
a=rtpmap:96 H.264/90000
a=rtpmap:98 rtx/90000
a=fmtp:98 apt=96;rtx-time=3000
a=ssrc-group:FID 11111 22222
a=ssrc:11111 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc:22222 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc-group:FID 33333 44444
a=ssrc:33333 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc:44444 cname:user3@example.com

That prevents the complexity of associating original sources with retransmission sources when SSRC multiplexing is used for RTP retransmission.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples go from the simplest case, one source in an audio stream, through one participant sending two cameras from the same stream, to two pairs of sources where each pair is marked as a retransmission relationship.

sections.title: Offer/Answer and Older Receivers
sections.content:
When used with the SDP offer/answer model, source-specific attributes describe only the sources that each party is willing to send, whether it is sending RTP data or RTCP report blocks. No mechanism is provided by which an answer can accept or reject individual sources within a media stream; if the set of sources in a media stream is unacceptable, the answerer's only option is to reject the media stream or the entire multimedia session.

The SSRC identifiers for sources described by an SDP answer MUST be distinct from the identifiers for sources of that media stream in the offer. Similarly, new SSRC identifiers in an updated offer MUST be distinct from the identifiers for that media stream established in the most recent offer/answer exchange, and SHOULD be distinct from any identifier ever used by either party within the multimedia session, whether or not it is still being used.

According to the definition of SDP, interpreters of session descriptions ignore unknown attributes. Endpoints MUST therefore be prepared for the fact that recipients of their RTP media session may not understand their explicit source descriptions, unless some external mechanism indicates that they were understood. In some cases, such as RTP retransmission, this may constrain some choices about the bitstreams that are transmitted.

Source descriptions are specified in this document such that RTP endpoints that are compliant with the RTP specification will be able to decode the media streams they describe whether or not they support explicit source descriptions. However, some deployed RTP implementations may not actually support multiple media sources in a media stream. Media senders MAY therefore wish to restrict themselves to a single source at a time unless they have some means of concluding that the receivers of the media stream support source multiplexing.
sections.plainLanguage:
In an offer and answer, the source lines only say what each side is willing to send. There is no way to accept some sources and refuse others, so a receiver that dislikes the list has to refuse the whole stream.

And because SDP readers skip lines they do not recognise, a sender cannot count on its source lines being read. It should keep to one source unless it has some other way of knowing the receiver can handle several.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: All the security implications of RTP and of SDP apply. Explicitly describing the multiplexed sources of an RTP media stream does not appear to add any further security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Describing the sources inside a stream does not add anything new to the security picture; the same rules that apply to RTP and to SDP already cover it.
